clue.text: God involved in aggressive act by desperately ill conman as president (7,7)

indicators.note: To be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, and that is where the god's two letters end up.
A desperate scramble is the opposite of an orderly one, so nothing that follows stays in the order the clue gives it.

blocks.note: ABH is actual bodily harm, the charge sheet's name for an assault
Ra, the Egyptian sun god, is the crossword's favourite deity
the nine letters of ILL CONMAN in a thoroughly desperate state

explanation.walkthrough: ABH is police shorthand for actual bodily harm, which is the aggressive act you are asked to picture. The crooked politician of the surface is pure misdirection: the man wanted here is the honest one.
explanation.definitionFit: president → ABRAHAM LINCOLN: definition by example, one named holder of the office standing in for the office itself.

clue.text: I trace criminal drilling behind cell (9)

indicators.note: Criminal here means bent rather than lawbreaking, and letters that have gone bent will not sit in their proper order.
Drilling is boring a way into something, so what it touches ends up inside the word next to it.

blocks.note: the behind you sit on
the six letters of I TRACE rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' is the body part, not a position — the one word that looks like a positional instruction and is really fodder. The definition, for once, is literal biology rather than a prison joke.
explanation.definitionFit: cell → BACTERIUM: a bacterium is one entire organism built of a single cell, so 'cell' names it by everything it consists of.

clue.text: Scene of conflict a long while back (5)

indicators.note: Back asks you to read the words the other way round, from their last letter towards their first.

blocks.note: an era is a long while, and these five letters are the whole of the wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' is not an article propping up the sentence but a letter you write down, which is what makes such a short wordplay so easy to walk past.
explanation.definitionFit: Scene of conflict → ARENA: the sand-floored ring where Roman fights were staged, now any place where a contest is fought out.

clue.text: Had a go at casual worker after attending inspirational talk (9)

indicators.note: After is a positional word, not a mixing one: whatever it introduces has already been written down when the next piece arrives.

blocks.note: to attend something is to be at it
a temp is the office's casual worker, hired by the week
a TED talk is the modern byword for an inspirational talk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspirational talk' is the giveaway: TED has become the generic name for one, so a setter can call on it without ever printing the capitals.
explanation.definitionFit: Had a go at → ATTEMPTED: both are past-tense ways of saying you tried something, with the clue's version the more casual of the two.

clue.text: Private area's security measures no good (5)

definitions.note: The answer is a plural word for a single region of the body, so the singular 'area' fits the place even though the word itself counts as more than one.

indicators.note: 'No' refuses something entry, so the letter it names is taken straight back out of what precedes it.

blocks.note: logins are the security measures guarding a computer
G is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report

explanation.walkthrough: A deletion clue makes you name the letter that leaves, and here it is G for good. The surface reads as a gated garden, which is exactly what it is meant to.
explanation.definitionFit: Private area → LOINS: the loins are the region between hip and groin, the decorous biblical word for the part of the body nobody names directly.

clue.text: Damaged manicure on left of digits (9)

indicators.note: Damaged goods have lost their proper shape, and so have these letters — not one of them stays where the clue put it.
This is a down entry, so 'on' is vertical: the piece named first sits on top of the one named next.

blocks.note: the eight letters of MANICURE in a new order
L is the everyday abbreviation for left

explanation.walkthrough: Digits are fingers on the surface — hence the manicure — and numbers in the definition. That double sense is the joke, and it is why the nail bar looks like part of the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: of digits → NUMERICAL: numerical means expressed in numbers, and a digit is a single number, the sense that has nothing to do with fingers.

clue.text: Share view of deforestation's impact? (5)

blocks.note: count the trees left standing once the loggers have finished: zero, which is written O
deforestation leaves nothing where the PINE trees stood; that 'nothing' is spelled with the letter O, placed directly before PINE to build the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words and the question mark explains itself: it is a picture of what is missing, not a description of a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Share view → OPINE: to opine is to state an opinion, a faintly formal verb for offering other people what you think.

clue.text: Not one in three, sadly (7)

indicators.note: A thing done sadly is a thing done badly, and badly handled letters finish up in the wrong places.

blocks.note: the seven letters of IN THREE, sadly rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not one in three' reads as a statistic, and that is the trap — the numbers are letters. The answer counts two things, not three, so the surface even has the arithmetic wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Not one → NEITHER: the word means not one of two possibilities, so the definition works once you supply the 'of the two' it leaves out.

clue.text: Impart knowledge during class (6)

blocks.note: during the war, in the war — the two prepositions do the same job
a form is a school class, as in sixth form

explanation.walkthrough: British schools number their classes as forms, a convention setters lean on constantly. Nothing here misleads you: the surface picture and the wordplay are made of the same classroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Impart knowledge → INFORM: to inform someone is to pass on what you know, the plain synonym rather than the sense of shaping something.

clue.text: Mediterranean resort with hotel in bay (5)

indicators.note: 'In' is the plainest container word there is: the letter it introduces goes inside the word beside it, not next to it.

blocks.note: Nice is the resort on the Cote d'Azur
H is hotel in the NATO alphabet, the pilot's H

explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the NATO alphabet is fair game, and 'hotel' is among the busiest. 'Bay' is architectural here — an alcove in a wall — though the surface would much rather you saw the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: bay → NICHE: in a building a bay is a recess set back into a wall, which is just what a niche is, the shelf-sized hollow that holds a statue.

clue.text: Edging around spot of unrest, runs into seven Roman rulers (9)

indicators.note: Around is a wrapping word: the edging goes right the way round whatever comes next.
A spot of something is the smallest dab of it, and the smallest dab of a word is the letter it starts with.
Into burrows rather than joins, so what it governs is pushed inside the number instead of being tacked on the end.

blocks.note: trim is the edging sewn round a garment
the spot taken off the front of UNREST
seven written as Roman numerals, which the surface quietly recommends
R is the cricket scoreboard's abbreviation for runs

explanation.walkthrough: There are two separate wrappings here and the second is disguised as a number. 'Roman' earns its keep twice over, pointing at the numerals as well as at the men in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman rulers → TRIUMVIRI: the Latin plural of triumvir, one of the three men who between them held supreme power in Rome.

clue.text: Offer excessive backing for military service action? (7)

blocks.note: over- is the prefix English puts in front of anything done to excess
to arm a service is to back it with weapons, and an arm is also a branch of the forces

explanation.walkthrough: Both cricket and tennis use the word — a bowler delivers this way and a server strikes this way — which is why the definition can be so vague and still be fair.
explanation.definitionFit: action? → OVERARM: the question mark admits the looseness — the answer names the style of a bowling or serving action, the arm swung above the shoulder.

clue.text: Check behind rocks for possible sign of distress (7)

indicators.note: Behind is positional: the piece it governs is written last, tucked in at the back of what came first.

blocks.note: scree is the loose rock that slides down a mountainside
ch. is the chess notation for check

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' looks like an instruction to shake the letters up and is nothing of the kind — it is stone, doing straight duty. Chess supplies the CH, an abbreviation worth memorising.
explanation.definitionFit: possible sign of distress → SCREECH: a screech is the noise someone in trouble makes, and 'possible' concedes it might equally be brakes or an owl.

clue.text: Hardline communist, not a wet (5)

indicators.note: 'Not' cancels whatever follows it, so the letter named next is struck out of the longer word.

blocks.note: a Maoist follows Mao's hardline brand of communism
the single letter the clue asks you to take out

explanation.walkthrough: The letter that leaves is hiding as the humble 'a', which is why it is so easy to read past. 'Wet' is a political word too — a soft Tory — so the whole surface hangs together.
explanation.definitionFit: wet → MOIST: a plain synonym, though the answer is the damper, more clinging end of wet rather than soaked through.

clue.text: Jazz on electronic record label (9)

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so 'on' means sitting above: the jazz goes on top of everything that follows it.

blocks.note: trad is the traditional New Orleans jazz of Acker Bilk
e- is the prefix for anything electronic, as in email
to mark something down is to record it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' is a verb here, not the vinyl the jazz invites you to imagine, and that switch is the whole difficulty. Trad and e- are both conventions you will meet again next week.
explanation.definitionFit: label → TRADEMARK: the registered name or symbol a firm puts on its goods, so 'label' names it by the job it does on the packaging.

clue.text: Keep holding note, intermittently acerbic, for old newsreader (4,5)

indicators.note: Holding is what a container does: the keep hangs on to the other pieces rather than standing beside them.
Something done intermittently happens every other time, so you take every other letter of the word next to it.

blocks.note: the keep of a castle is its central tower
n. is the dictionary's abbreviation for a note
every other letter of aCeRbIc

explanation.walkthrough: A keep is a castle's tower, and what it holds is two unrelated scraps rather than one word. 'Old newsreader' is the joke: this man read the news in the street centuries before television existed.
explanation.definitionFit: old newsreader → TOWN CRIER: before newspapers he walked the streets calling out proclamations, so he read the news in the oldest sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Effort to get section of Commons supporting Labour platform (9)

indicators.note: To support is to hold up from below, and in a down entry below means later, at the foot of the answer.

blocks.note: work is effort, the noun rather than the job
MPs sit on the front and back benches of the Commons

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all Westminster and the answer is all carpentry. The capital L on Labour is the misdirection: the definition wants labour with a small one, the kind done by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour platform → WORKBENCH: the raised surface you labour at, so 'platform' is literal and 'Labour' is work with the politics stripped out of it.

clue.text: Point to pet I claim is abandoned (9)

indicators.note: Abandoned means unrestrained rather than deserted, and letters with nothing restraining them will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: the nine letters of PET I CLAIM, thoroughly rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The setter needs 'is' to make the sentence work and it carries nothing; everything either side of it is either the fodder or the signal to shake it.
explanation.definitionFit: Point to → IMPLICATE: to implicate someone is to indicate their involvement in wrongdoing, so 'point to' catches the finger-pointing without the courtroom.

clue.text: Officer's subordinate losing head after signal to pause (9)

indicators.note: Losing your head takes the first letter off, because the head of a word is the end it starts at.
After is positional: the trimmed word is written second, behind the piece the clue names next.

blocks.note: a comma is the punctuation mark that signals a pause
an underling is under you, and the U at its head is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: A comma really is the signal to pause, which is a nice piece of punctuation as vocabulary. Beheadings always take the first letter — no clue ever means the last one by 'head'.
explanation.definitionFit: Officer → COMMANDER: definition by example, since a commander is one particular naval rank and 'officer' is the general word covering it.

clue.text: Gratuities dry up where turds gather? (7)

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so 'up' reads from the bottom of the answer towards the top, turning the letters round.

blocks.note: tips are the gratuities left on a table
sec is what a French wine label calls dry

explanation.walkthrough: Sec for dry is worth learning — setters use it constantly, and it never announces that it is French. The question mark apologises for a definition that describes rather than translates.
explanation.definitionFit: where turds gather → CESSPIT: a cesspit is the covered pit a household's sewage drains into, so the clue defines the place by its contents.

clue.text: 50-50 about a sports jacket feature (5)

indicators.note: About means round the outside, so the two numerals end up sitting either side of what follows them.

blocks.note: L is fifty in Roman numerals, and the clue asks for it twice
the letter taken straight out of the clue
PE is what a school timetable calls sport

explanation.walkthrough: '50-50' looks like odds and is really two Roman fifties. PE for sport comes off a timetable and is one of the most reliable two-letter fillers a setter owns.
explanation.definitionFit: jacket feature → LAPEL: the folded flap at the front of a jacket collar, so the definition names the garment and leaves you to find the part.

clue.text: Rubbish batch of small buns? (6)

blocks.note: the crisp packets and cans dropped in a park
bun is an old word for a rabbit, and a doe's young all arrive at once

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated senses share one word, and the second is well buried: 'bun' for a rabbit is old dialect, which is what the setter's question mark is apologising for.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish → LITTER, the stuff dropped in the street; and 'bun' is an old word for a rabbit, so a batch of small ones is a litter.

clue.text: Ease when floating, for example, among marine mammals (3,4)

indicators.note: Among puts a thing in the middle of a group, so the short piece lands inside the longer one rather than after it.

blocks.note: seals are marine mammals, the ones barking on the rocks
eg is the standard abbreviation for 'for example', from the Latin exempli gratia

explanation.walkthrough: EG is a workhorse abbreviation and here it hides in plain sight as part of the sentence. The definition is an idiom: you get yours after a day of not falling over.
explanation.definitionFit: Ease when floating → SEA LEGS: yours are the knack of walking steadily on a rolling deck, so the phrase names the comfort a passenger gains at sea.

clue.text: Portion of filo I added, served up as garnish (5)

indicators.note: A portion is a part and not the whole, so only some of the letters that follow are wanted — and consecutive ones at that.
This is a down entry, so 'up' reads the letters from the bottom towards the top, which is backwards from how they are printed.

blocks.note: filO I Added conceals five consecutive letters, waiting to be turned round

explanation.walkthrough: Finding the run of letters is only half the job.
explanation.definitionFit: garnish → AIOLI: the garlic mayonnaise spooned alongside fish or vegetables, so 'garnish' names it by the job it does on the plate.

clue.text: Doesn't go to sleep on board ship (5)

indicators.note: Being on board is being inside the vessel, so what follows goes within the ship rather than alongside it.

blocks.note: SS is the steamship prefix painted on a hull
a kip is British slang for a sleep

explanation.walkthrough: Kip and SS are both everyday crossword currency, and the surface they build — sleeping aboard — is exactly the picture they describe. Only the definition is pulling the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Doesn't go → SKIPS: to skip a meeting is to miss it on purpose, so the answer is the verb for deciding not to turn up.

clue.text: Splitting chocolate bar to be eaten by hazard (7)

definitions.note: 'Splitting' is a participle where the answer is a preposition; both stand between two things, which is the sense that lets the setter swap one for the other.

indicators.note: Being eaten by something puts you inside it, so the bar goes within the word that swallows it.

blocks.note: to hazard money is to bet it
Twix is the two-finger chocolate bar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazard' is a verb here — to risk — not the danger it looks like. And a brand name is fair game: setters treat a chocolate bar as ordinary vocabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: Splitting → BETWIXT: an archaic form of between, and a thing that splits two others is standing between them.

clue.text: Right winger the heart of Athletic (5)

indicators.note: The heart of a word is its middle, so you keep only the letters at its centre and drop what is either side.

blocks.note: a tit is a small bird, and a bird is a thing with wings
the two letters at the centre of athLEtic

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right winger' reads as politics or football and is really two separate jobs bolted together — the definition stops after a single word. Athletic is a football club on the surface, which hides the split beautifully.
explanation.definitionFit: Right → TITLE: in law your title to a house is your right of ownership, a sense that survives mostly in the phrase 'title deeds'.

clue.text: Way of putting one's foot down in support of country (9)

definitions.text: Way of putting one's foot down

blocks.note: pro means in favour of, as in pro-European
a nation is a country thought of as its people

explanation.walkthrough: PRO for 'in support of' turns up constantly — pro-democracy, pro-am — and it is the only abbreviation in play. The difficulty is all in the definition, which describes rather than translates.
explanation.definitionFit: Way of putting one's foot down → PRONATION: the inward roll of the ankle as the foot lands, a runner's technical term hiding behind an idiom about being firm.

clue.text: Lord of most of Kent region (5)

indicators.note: Most of a word is all but the end of it, so the final letter never gets written down.

blocks.note: the Isle of Thanet is the north-east corner of Kent, where Margate and Ramsgate sit

explanation.walkthrough: Thanet is the whole clue once you spot it, and it is the sort of place name worth collecting. Macbeth supplies the definition — he was Thane of Cawdor before he was anything worse.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord → THANE: an Anglo-Saxon or Scottish noble who held his land from the king, so 'lord' is the modern word for the rank.

clue.text: Fat fool keeping almost emaciated First Lady very close (5,2,7)

indicators.note: To keep something is to hang on to it, so the fool wraps himself round the pieces that follow instead of standing beside them.
Almost means not quite all of it, so the last letter of the word next to it never arrives.

blocks.note: thick is fat when you are describing a slice of bread
an ass is a fool
thin, with its last letter never written
Eve was the first lady of all, long before any president had one

explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' points at Washington on the surface and at Eden underneath. The phrase means close in the sense of confiding in each other, never close in distance.
explanation.definitionFit: very close → THICK AS THIEVES: the idiom describes two people so intimate that they share secrets, which is closeness of friendship rather than of space.
